page: Google Cloud Platform n1-highmem-2 is a memory-allocated virtual machine instance belonging to the N1 machine family. It features 2 vCPUs mapped to 1 physical Intel Xeon core with hyper-threading enabled, running at a base clock speed of 2.3 GHz. The instance is equipped with 13.0 GB of system memory, yielding a memory-to-vCPU ratio of 6.5 GB per vCPU. It does not include local storage or bundled GPUs, and has zero complimentary public IPv4 addresses.

Performance benchmarks position this instance in the lower tiers for compute and memory throughput. The single-core stress-ng score of 1105.58 and Geekbench single-core score of 944.0 fall into the bottom 25%, while multi-core metrics like the stress-ng multi-core score of 1452.88 and Geekbench multi-core score of 1124.0 reside in the bottom 10%. Memory bandwidth tests show 80.89 GB/sec for cached small blocks and 13.32 GB/sec for uncached large blocks, reflecting its older-generation hardware architecture.

From a cost-efficiency perspective, the n1-highmem-2 offers a budget-friendly entry point for memory-intensive workloads that do not demand high-performance compute resources. The trade-off is lower processing speed and memory bandwidth in exchange for a larger memory footprint per vCPU. This configuration is suitable for small databases, in-memory caching layers, basic web serving, and lightweight background tasks requiring more RAM than processing power.
description: Google Cloud Platform n1-highmem-2 is an x86_64 virtual machine featuring 2 vCPUs and 13.0 GB of RAM, powered by an Intel Xeon processor running at 2.3 GHz. Lacking local storage and GPU accelerators, this instance is designed for memory-allocated workloads. Benchmark results indicate modest performance, with single-core and multi-core CPU scores falling in the bottom 25% and 10% respectively, and memory bandwidth reaching 13.32 GB/sec for large uncached blocks. This instance provides a qualitative balance of high memory density relative to its low compute capacity, making it a cost-effective option for workloads that are constrained by memory capacity rather than CPU performance. It is best suited for small databases, caching layers, and lightweight memory-bound applications.
